Chapter 2: The Roots of Inequality — Religion and the Making of Caste.
When we try to make sense of why our world is divided the way it is, we often turn to stories—stories that have been passed down through generations. In India, a lot of these stories come straight from religious texts, seen as the final word on how society should be set up.
For people who benefit from the caste system, these ancient words act like a shield. They use them to justify their privilege, keeping others in their place—sometimes without even realizing they're doing it.
Picture this: a young man, troubled by why his family is always treated as outsiders, turns to his grandfather for answers. The old man opens a battered scripture and starts reciting lines about how society was born from the body of a cosmic being—priests from the mouth, warriors from the arms, merchants from the thighs, and laborers from the feet. And anyone outside this order? They're left nameless, faceless—doomed to serve, without hope for change.
What really comes through is that the caste system isn't just about social rules—it's wrapped up in religion. These rules aren’t enforced just out of habit, but carry the weight of divine command. The scriptures don’t just describe life as it is; they lay out how it should be, making it nearly impossible to question the system without also questioning the authority of religion.
Most people don’t even notice how deep these beliefs run in everyday life. Think about it—the rituals for birth, marriage, or even a funeral, all shaped by caste. The prayers said in temples, the festivals filling the streets, the food on your plate—caste touches it all. For folks at the top, religion can be comforting, a source of certainty. But for people at the bottom, it brings pain and exclusion.
And then, there are moments when the injustice of it all is impossible to ignore. Imagine a group of children, excited to learn, but turned away from school because of their caste. Or a woman, desperate for water, beaten just for crossing an invisible line at the village well. In these moments, the cruelty of the system is undeniable—and the stories used to justify it start to unravel.
Some people argue that caste is just a matter of social convenience, a practical way to organize labor and keep order. But the truth? It’s a system of domination, propped up by the threat of religious punishment. Breaking the rules doesn’t just mean being left out socially—it means fearing punishment from above.
So, what does real change look like? It starts by challenging the religious ideas that keep inequality locked in place. As long as the scriptures are treated as beyond question, the caste system stays strong. True change needs courage—not just to question the rules, but to question the beliefs that give those rules their power.
